messages.content:
Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Depression scores on the HADs improved significantly more with vitamin D3 than with placebo in IBS-D patients.
Sentence: "Symptoms severity, QoL, HADs-depression, and VSI score improved significantly in the vitamin D group as compared to the placebo group (P-values: <0.001, 0.049, 0.023, and 0.008; respectively)."
Measured as: HADs-depression score
Population: Adults aged 18-65 with diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome
Intervention: Vitamin D3 50,000 IU/week for 9 weeks
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 74
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation did not differ from placebo in seasonal affective symptom scores (SIGH-SAD) at 12 weeks.
Sentence: "There were no significant between-group differences in SIGH-SAD sums at 12 weeks (p = 0.7 (CI: - 3.27 to 4.81))."
Measured as: SIGH-SAD sum
Population: Healthcare professionals with seasonal affective symptoms (SPAQ-SAD question 2 score of 8 or more)
Intervention: 70 μg vitamin D daily for 3 months
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 50
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"Both are placebo-controlled vitamin D RCTs on depressive symptoms but in different populations (IBS-D patients vs healthcare workers with seasonal affective symptoms), with different doses and scales; the results genuinely differ.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"population","also_differs":["intervention","outcome_measure"],"detail":"population: IBS-D patients (HADs, 50,000 IU/week x 9 wks) vs healthcare professionals with seasonal affective symptoms (SIGH-SAD, 70 μg daily x 12 wks)"}
